title: H-1B Workers Now Make Up 4.3% of America's AI Workforce, EIG Finds
excerpt: Analysis by the Economic Innovation Group shows immigrant workers are disproportionately vital to the U.S. AI talent base, and proposes a wage-ranking visa system that could triple AI admissions.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • H-1B visa holders make up 4.3% of the U.S. AI workforce, significantly higher than AI's overall job share.
  • 80% of H-1B workers in AI graduated from U.S. universities, earning an average wage of $150,000.
  • EIG's wage-ranking proposal could increase annual AI H-1B admissions from 1,000 to 3,330.
  • U.S. immigration policy changes may push skilled AI workers to countries like China.
  • 65% of top AI companies in the U.S. have at least one immigrant founder.

  • H-1B visa holders now represent 4.3% of the total U.S. AI workforce, far exceeding AI's 0.06% share of all American jobs, according to the Economic Innovation Group.
  • Nearly four out of five H-1B holders working in AI completed their education at American universities, earning a mean wage of $150,000.
  • EIG's proposed wage-ranking system could triple the number of AI workers admitted annually from roughly 1,000 to 3,330.
  • The findings arrive as China ramps up AI talent recruitment and U.S. policy changes — including a now-struck-down $100,000 visa fee — threaten to push skilled workers abroad.

H-1B visa holders have become a critical pillar of the American artificial intelligence workforce, accounting for 4.3 percent of all AI workers in the country, according to a new analysis by the Economic Innovation Group, a bipartisan research and advocacy organization in Washington, D.C.

https://x.com/faith3155/status/2078251398206992618

The research, published on EIG's Agglomerations blog, draws on Freedom of Information Act data on H-1B approvals and finds that nearly 1,000 workers who received H-1B visas in fiscal year 2024 were employed in AI-related occupations. That represents 1.12 percent of all approvals — a small figure on its face, but roughly 19 times AI's share of the broader U.S. labor market, where the sector accounts for just 0.06 percent of all jobs.

A Workforce Built on Immigrant Talent

The EIG data underscores the degree to which the American AI industry depends on foreign-born talent. Nearly 80 percent of new H-1B holders working in AI completed their education at American universities, compared to 52 percent of H-1B holders overall. These workers earn a mean wage of $150,000 — 37 percent above the average for all H-1B visa holders.

"Losing many of these workers to China would undermine the domestic AI industry and could threaten American national security."

— Economic Innovation Group

"The average federal fiscal impact per worker would climb from $38,000 to $44,000 annually."

"The average federal fiscal impact per worker would climb from $38,000 to $44,000 annually."

The reliance on immigrant founders runs even deeper. According to the National Foundation for American Policy, 65 percent of the top 43 AI companies in the United States have at least one immigrant founder. Some 70 percent of full-time graduate students in AI-related fields at American universities come from abroad.

A Wage-Ranking Fix

EIG's central policy proposal is to replace the current H-1B lottery with a wage-ranking system that would prioritize applicants by their actual salary offers rather than occupation-specific wage levels. Had such a system been in place for fiscal year 2024, the number of AI workers admitted on H-1B visas would have more than tripled — from roughly 1,000 to 3,330, according to EIG's simulations.

Under the proposed system, the mean wage for H-1B AI workers would rise from $150,000 to $169,000. The average federal fiscal impact per worker would climb from $38,000 to $44,000 annually. The share of new H-1B recipients working in AI would have been 3.9 percent in 2024, up from 1.1 percent under the current lottery.

EIG has argued that the current lottery-based system favors large tech firms and relies on easily manipulated occupational classifications, which can allow IT outsourcing companies to absorb a disproportionate share of visas.

Policy Turbulence

The analysis arrives during a period of intense upheaval in U.S. immigration policy. In September 2025, President Trump imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa applications, a move aimed at deterring foreign hiring. A federal judge in Boston struck down the fee in June 2026, ruling it constituted an unlawful tax that Congress never authorized. The administration has said it will appeal.

A PitchBook analysis found that the fee, while in effect, widened the divide between well-capitalized AI labs and smaller startups. OpenAI landed 27 H-1B approvals in the first half of fiscal 2026, already surpassing its full-year fiscal 2025 total of 21. Anthropic, meanwhile, relied almost entirely on internal H-1B transfers from other companies rather than new applications, according to federal data.

The Department of Homeland Security has also proposed a weighted lottery that would give applicants in higher wage levels better odds of selection. EIG has criticized this approach, arguing it would actually increase visa awards to IT outsourcing firms and create new incentives for employers to misclassify workers into lower-paying occupation codes.

The China Competition

EIG's report explicitly frames the H-1B question as a national security issue. Last August, the Chinese State Council announced its most comprehensive AI policy initiative to date, directing enterprises to attract skilled workers through equity incentives and stock options. China has also introduced a new visa category for foreign STEM graduates.

Meanwhile, the White House's recent AI Legislative Framework makes no mention of workforce support. EIG warns that without reforms to attract and retain AI talent, the United States risks ceding ground in a competition with direct security implications.

What's Next

The future of the H-1B program remains in flux. The administration's appeal of the $100,000 fee ruling is pending. DHS's proposed weighted lottery rule is undergoing public comment, with EIG and other groups pushing for an occupation-agnostic, compensation-based ranking instead.

For the roughly 730,000 H-1B holders currently in the United States, the policy direction will determine whether America's AI talent pipeline grows or contracts. As EIG puts it, in a labor market where annual flows of 1,000 high-skilled workers have an outsized competitive impact, the stakes of getting visa reform right are disproportionately high.
